title: Question 12
stem:
An X-ray beam is used to produce an image of a model of a thumb.
A parallel beam of X-ray radiation of intensity $I_0$ is incident on the model, as illustrated in Fig. 12.1.
{{figure:figure_12_1}}
Fig. 12.1
Data for the attenuation (absorption) coefficient $\mu$ in bone and in soft tissue are shown in Fig. 12.2.
{{figure:figure_12_2}}
Fig. 12.2

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: Calculate, in terms of the incident intensity $I_0$ of the X-ray beam, the intensity of the beam after passing through
parts.text: a thickness of $2.8\text{ cm}$ of soft tissue,
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 12.2 for the soft tissue value and Fig. 12.1 for the distance travelled. Think about whether each extra centimetre removes the same fraction of whatever intensity is left.
Hint 2: Use the exponential law for one material with $\mu = 0.90\text{ cm}^{-1}$ and $x = 2.8\text{ cm}$, leaving $I_0$ as a symbol to find the transmitted fraction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture How Attenuation Works**
Think of the beam losing a fixed fraction in each thin slice. That gives an exponential fall, not a straight line fall. For a single uniform material the transmitted intensity depends on the starting intensity $I_0$, the material constant $\mu$ and the thickness $x$.

Step 2: **Put In The Soft Tissue Numbers**
For soft tissue only:
$$I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}$$
$$I = I_0 \exp(-0.90 \times 2.8)$$
$$I = I_0 \exp(-2.52)$$
$$I = 0.080 I_0$$
So only about 8% gets through 2.8 cm of soft tissue.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: the bone and soft tissue, as shown in Fig. 12.1.
hints: Hint 1: Trace the central ray through Fig. 12.1. Part of the total 2.8 cm is now bone of thickness 1.3 cm, so work out how much soft tissue thickness is left on that path.

Hint 2: Treat the beam as attenuated first by soft tissue and then by bone. Use $\mu = 0.90\text{ cm}^{-1}$ for 1.5 cm of tissue and $\mu = 3.0\text{ cm}^{-1}$ for 1.3 cm of bone, then combine the two factors.
parts.proper_answer: Soft tissue thickness $= 2.8 - 1.3 = 1.5\text{ cm}$. $I = I_0 e^{-0.90 \times 1.5} e^{-3.0 \times 1.3} = 0.0052 I_0$
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Split The Path Into Two Parts**
The ray still travels 2.8 cm in total, but 1.3 cm of that is bone. That leaves:
$$x_{tissue} = 2.8 - 1.3 = 1.5\text{ cm}$$
$$x_{bone} = 1.3\text{ cm}$$
Bone absorbs much more strongly because its $\mu$ is larger.

Step 2: **Combine Two Exponential Falls**
Attenuation happens in succession, so the fractions multiply:
$$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu_{tissue}x_{tissue}) \times \exp(-\mu_{bone}x_{bone})$$
$$I = I_0 \exp(-0.90 \times 1.5) \times \exp(-3.0 \times 1.3)$$
$$I = I_0 \times 0.259 \times 0.0202$$
$$I = 0.0052 I_0$$
The bone path transmits far less than the tissue-only path.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by the *contrast* of an X-ray image.

markscheme_points.text: difference in degrees of blackening between structures

hints: Hint 1: Picture the developed X-ray film. Some regions look dark and some look pale - think about what you are comparing between two neighbouring patches.
Hint 2: Link that visual difference to the physics - it comes from the difference in detected intensity after passing through different structures.
parts.proper_answer: Contrast is the difference in degree of blackening (or in transmitted X-ray intensity) between different structures / adjacent areas of the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What You See On The Film**
Where more X-rays get through, the film is blackened more. Where bone blocks X-rays, the film stays paler. Contrast describes how distinct those light and dark regions are from each other.

Step 2: **Clean Definition To Use**
Contrast is the difference in degree of blackening between structures, corresponding to the difference in transmitted intensities for different tissues. Good imaging needs neighbouring tissues to give clearly different blackening.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: By reference to your answers in (a), suggest whether the X-ray image of the model has good contrast.

markscheme_points.text: large difference in intensities so goc

hints: Hint 1: Compare your two fractions from (a), about $0.080 I_0$ and $0.0052 I_0$ - is one very much larger than the other, giving very different blackening?
parts.proper_answer: Yes, good contrast, because there is a large difference / ratio between the two transmitted intensities ($0.080 I_0$ compared with $0.0052 I_0$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Judge The Difference**
From (a) the tissue-only intensity is about $0.080 I_0$ while the bone-plus-tissue intensity is about $0.0052 I_0$, a factor of about 15 difference.
$$\frac{0.080}{0.0052} \approx 15$$
That large difference in intensity gives a large difference in blackening, so bone stands out clearly from soft tissue. That means good contrast.
